rounds.hypothesis: Per diagnose.json: one defect in `copy_iovs_and_convert` (kernel/src/util/iovec.rs) conflates two rules in `IoVec::is_empty` = `len == 0 || base == 0`. The `base == 0` clause makes a {NULL, 1024} buffer look absent, so it is filtered out and never converted, and the page fault that Linux relies on to produce EFAULT never happens (cases 1 and 2 return 0). The `len == 0` clause legitimately identifies {usize::MAX, 0} as empty, but `continue` skips it before anything range-checks the base, so an out-of-range address is never seen (case 3 copies 284 bytes instead of failing). Fix per suggested_direction: drop the `base == 0` clause so a null base is no longer a special case, and range-check every entry -- including empty ones -- before any entry is converted.
rounds.change: kernel/src/util/iovec.rs only. (a) `IoVec::is_empty` is now `self.len == 0`; the `|| self.base == 0` clause is gone, with a doc comment pointing at the delayed-validation contract in `CurrentUserSpace::reader`. (b) Added `IoVec::check_range`, which applies the same `base.saturating_add(len) > MAX_USERSPACE_VADDR => EFAULT` predicate that `VmSpace::reader`/`writer` already use, so the eager check can never disagree with the lazy one. (c) Restructured `copy_iovs_and_convert` into three passes: copy and length-validate the whole vector, then `check_range` every entry, then truncate/filter/convert. Nothing else changed -- the `MAX_TOTAL_IOV_BYTES` truncation and the documented no-empty-readers invariant relied on by preadv.rs:157 and pwritev.rs:106 are intact. Deleted the three target lines from blocklists/readv_test, and extended the existing test/initramfs/src/regression/io/file_io/iovec_err.c with a `bad_iov_base` case covering both directions.
rounds.outcome: green: `All conformance tests passed.`, make exit 0, 3/3 passed, matching the host prebuilt exactly. Confirmed in the same binary that all 31 ReadvTest cases pass, including the three guards diagnose.json named (NullIovecInNonemptyArray, ZeroIovecs_File, ZeroIovecs_Pipe). `make check` clean, `make docs` clean, full AUTO_TEST=regression green.

rounds.hypothesis: Not a new failure -- a self-review round. My first cut called `check_range` inside the single existing loop, which meant entry N's base was validated before entry N+1's length. Linux splits these across two functions (`iovec_from_user` validates lengths, `__import_iovec` validates bases), so the relative order is observable and my version could report EFAULT where Linux reports EINVAL.
rounds.change: Confirmed the divergence against the host with a scratch probe (/tmp/iov_order.c, deleted): for {base=-1, len=0} + {base=valid, len=negative}, Linux returns EINVAL in both entry orders, whereas my single-pass version returned EFAULT when the bad base came first -- a regression against the pre-change code, which returned EINVAL. Split the loop so every length is validated before any base is, and asserted both orders in the new regression case.
rounds.outcome: Fixed before it ever shipped. Re-ran the target filter (3/3 green), the nine-case guard filter (9/9 green), `make check`, and the full regression suite -- all green. The new `bad_iov_base` case scores 20/20 in Asterinas and 20/20 on the host.

rounds.hypothesis: Also not a new failure -- triage of two assertions in my own new regression case that failed in Asterinas while passing on the host. Both involve a faulting transfer against a ramfs file: a `writev` that reports EFAULT still leaves the file size expanded, and a `readv` at EOF with an unmapped buffer reports EFAULT instead of 0. The question that decides whether they belong to this fix: are they in the iovec import layer, or below it in ramfs/the page cache?
rounds.change: Isolated with a scratch probe (test/.../zzprobe.c, deleted) that used a *non-zero* mmap(PROT_NONE) base -- an address the pre-fix `is_empty` never filtered, so those paths behaved identically before my change. Ran it twice in Asterinas: once with the fix, once with `git checkout kernel/src/util/iovec.rs` and only the probe in place.
rounds.outcome: Both runs produced byte-identical output (11 passed, 6 failed), proving all six are pre-existing defects below the iovec layer -- ramfs `write_at` sets `inode_meta.size` before `page_cache.write` can fault, and `Vmo::read` faults on the writer before clamping to file size. Out of scope for this commit and deliberately not patched: fixing them means making ramfs writes transactional, a separate root cause at a different layer. Reordered my regression case so the two null-base EFAULT assertions come last and the ramfs size leak cannot poison later assertions; the case now passes 20/20 in Asterinas and 20/20 on the host, and asserts only what this layer owns.

layer: Matches diagnose.json's `owning_layer` exactly: the iovec import layer in kernel/src/util/iovec.rs::copy_iovs_and_convert. Nothing below it was touched. This is the right owner for two independent reasons. First, the invariant is all-or-nothing *across the vector* -- an out-of-range base in entry 1 must stop entry 0 from transferring -- and this function is the only place in Asterinas that sees the whole vector before any transfer, since there is no `iov_iter` equivalent. No per-entry consumer downstream can enforce it. Second, the two error classes have an observable relative order (all lengths before any base), which is a property of the vector, not of any entry. Deliberately not patched: `VmSpace::reader`/`writer` in ostd, which already implement the range check correctly and were simply never reached for filtered entries -- diagnose.json called this out and I confirmed it by reusing their exact predicate rather than inventing a second one. Also not patched: the six syscall entry points, which would each need the same fix.
generalizes:
The fix is a deletion of a special case plus a check applied uniformly to every entry, so there is no branch anywhere on the flag, size, errno, file type, or entry index this test happens to use. The word `readv` does not appear in the patch.

It fixes five callers the target test never exercises. All six sites share `copy_iovs_and_convert`: preadv.rs:90 (preadv/preadv2) and :155 (readv), pwritev.rs:91 (pwritev/pwritev2) and :151 (writev), and socket.rs:167/:178 (sendmsg/sendmmsg/recvmsg/recvmmsg). The write direction is the more serious half and had *no* suite coverage at all -- diagnose.json noted there is no writev_test binary in the prebuilts -- yet before this change `writev` with {base=NULL, len=n} reported 0 bytes written instead of EFAULT, which a caller retrying on a short write cannot distinguish from a full buffer. I verified the write side directly with a host probe covering both directions and 12 base/length combinations, and added the write-direction assertions to the committed regression case, so the half the conformance suite cannot see is now guarded in-tree.

Correctness beyond the test was checked against the host rather than assumed. A scratch probe (deleted) compared Linux and Asterinas on: null base at zero and non-zero length; out-of-range base at zero length in first and second position; a base ending exactly at the top of user space; a base straddling it; a base whose base+len wraps; and both ordering permutations of a bad base against a negative length. Asterinas now matches Linux on every one. Worth recording one boundary difference the probe surfaced: x86 Linux's `access_ok` rejects a zero-length base only above the sign bit (2^63), not above TASK_SIZE, so Linux accepts {base=2^47, len=0} while Asterinas rejects it against MAX_USERSPACE_VADDR. I chose to keep Asterinas's own boundary rather than transplant Linux's, because using MAX_USERSPACE_VADDR is what keeps the eager check and the lazy `VmSpace` check from disagreeing -- a second, looser predicate here would let a buffer pass import and then fail conversion. Every address in that gap is unmapped in Asterinas, so both kernels reject any *non-empty* buffer there; the divergence is confined to zero-length buffers, which transfer nothing either way. The gvisor case asserts the value the test actually uses, (void*)-1, which both boundaries reject.

The three in-tree guards diagnose.json named all still pass (NullIovecInNonemptyArray returns 284 rather than EFAULT, ZeroIovecs_File and ZeroIovecs_Pipe unchanged), plus BadIovecsPointer_File/_Pipe and the full 31-case ReadvTest binary. The socket callers are covered by the existing tcp_err/udp_err/msg_peek/msg_trunc/sendmmsg regression tests and the whole AUTO_TEST=regression suite is green. Two scope boundaries held deliberately: ReadvTestNoFixture.TruncatedAtMax stays blocked (unrelated, still fails), and ReadvTest.NotReadable_Pipe stays blocked despite being stale-green, per diagnose.json's instruction to keep this commit to one root cause.

One class of divergence found and deliberately left alone: six assertions about faulting transfers against ramfs files fail in Asterinas, and I proved by reverting the kernel diff and re-running the identical probe that they are byte-for-byte pre-existing, below this layer (ramfs `write_at` commits the new file size before `page_cache.write` can fault; `Vmo::read` faults on the writer before clamping to file size). They are a separate root cause at a separate layer and fixing them here would have made this commit two changes.
fix_summary:
Stops treating a null iovec base as an absent buffer, and range-checks every entry's base -- including zero-length entries -- before any entry transfers data.

The root cause was one predicate doing two jobs. `IoVec::is_empty` was `len == 0 || base == 0`, and the loop's `if iov.is_empty() { continue; }` used it both to skip buffers that transfer nothing and, accidentally, to skip validation. Those two clauses produced the two different wrong answers: the `base == 0` clause suppressed the very page fault Linux depends on for EFAULT, and the `len == 0` clause let an out-of-range address escape unexamined. So the fix is a separation, not an addition -- emptiness now means only `len == 0`, and range validation is a distinct step applied to all entries.

Designed against Asterinas's own abstractions in two places where they do not line up with Linux's. First, Asterinas has no `iov_iter`, so there is no `__import_iovec` to mirror; the equivalent seam is `copy_iovs_and_convert`, the one function that sees the whole vector before any conversion, and conversion is a pure `VmReader`/`VmWriter` construction that moves no data. That is what makes a plain early return give Linux's all-or-nothing behavior for free, with no rollback machinery. Second, for the range predicate I reused `VmSpace::reader`/`writer`'s existing `base.saturating_add(len) > MAX_USERSPACE_VADDR` rather than porting x86's `access_ok`. Reusing it is the load-bearing choice: the eager check and the lazy check are now the same rule, so no buffer can pass import and then fail conversion, which a hand-written second predicate would have allowed.

The fix also preserves two existing contracts rather than working around them. The documented delayed-buffer-validation design in `CurrentUserSpace::reader` -- which deliberately omits a lower-bound check so `read(fd, NULL, 1)` on an empty file returns 0 -- is what makes the null-base cases resolve to EFAULT naturally, at access time, instead of via an eager null rejection that would have broken it; the new `is_empty` doc comment records that dependency. And the invariant that the returned array holds no empty readers/writers is kept, so zero-length entries are still excluded after being validated and the `debug_assert!`s in preadv.rs and pwritev.rs still hold.

The three-pass structure is deliberate and its middle pass is not free: lengths are validated for the whole vector before any base is checked, because Linux splits those two jobs across `iovec_from_user` and `__import_iovec` and the resulting errno precedence is observable from userspace. My first version folded the base check into the existing single loop and got this wrong -- it reported EFAULT where Linux and the pre-change code both report EINVAL. A host probe caught it, and the committed regression case now pins both orderings so the structure cannot be collapsed back without a test failing.
